chunk_findings.detail: The write path stores whatever `array` typecodes the caller supplied (`ords.tobytes()` / `weights.tobytes()`), but the read path always reconstructs postings with `array("q")` and `array("d")`. Since `Postings` is only `tuple[array, array]`, a type-correct input such as `{"t": (array("i", [0]), array("f", [1.0]))}` is accepted by `index`, then `query` calls `array("q").frombytes` on the 4-byte ordinal blob and raises `ValueError: bytes length not a multiple of item size`; with an even number of `array("f")` weights it can silently return the wrong number/length of weights. The adapter therefore does not round-trip all valid `Postings` values.

chunk_findings.detail: `FakeSearchIndex.index` is implemented as a full replacement, identical to `rebuild`, so it discards all previously indexed documents and postings. For example: `fake.rebuild(None, [doc_a], {"a": postings_a})` followed by `fake.index(None, [doc_b], {"b": postings_b})` leaves `fake.docs == [doc_b]` and `fake.query(None, ["a", "b"])` returns only `{"b": postings_b}`. Since the `SearchIndex` port exposes both `index` and `rebuild`, a caller can reasonably use `index` to add a batch to an existing index; the fake silently loses prior state and therefore cannot faithfully exercise incremental indexing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/search.py:31

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier typecode mismatch still stands. `SqliteSearchIndex.index` writes whatever `array` typecodes the caller supplied (`ords.tobytes()` / `weights.tobytes()`), while `query` always reconstructs with the fixed constants `array(_ORD_TYPECODE)` / `array(_W_TYPECODE)` (`"q"` / `"d"`). The new constants do not pin the write path: they are not used or validated in `index`, and `Postings` remains the broad `tuple[array, array]`. For example, after `create`, calling `index(con, [], {"t": (array("i", [0]), array("f", [1.0]))})` stores a 4-byte ordinal blob; `query(con, ["t"])` then calls `array("q").frombytes(b"\x00\x00\x00\x00")` and raises `ValueError: bytes length not a multiple of item size`. With two `array("i")` ordinals the read can even succeed but return a bogus int64. Documentation that `"q"`/`"d"` are the only valid typecodes does not prevent this because the annotated public input still accepts and silently stores other array typecodes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/search.py:SqliteSearchIndex.index

chunk_findings.detail: `FakeSearchIndex.index()` overwrites the entire fake index instead of adding the newly indexed documents/postings to the existing state. For example, `fake.index(None, [doc1], {"a": {1}}); fake.index(None, [doc2], {"b": {2}})` leaves `self.docs == [doc2]` and `self.postings == {"b": {2}}`, so `fake.query(None, ["a"])` returns `{}` even though `doc1` was previously indexed. If callers/tests use the fake to simulate incremental indexing (the usual meaning of `index` when the port also has `rebuild`), this fake silently loses prior indexed data and can make tests pass or fail against the wrong semantics.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/search.py:31

chunk_findings.detail: `FakeSearchIndex.index` still does not append postings for a term that is already present; it replaces `self.postings[term]` with only the newly offset postings. For example, after `fake.rebuild(None, [doc0], {"a": (array("q", [0]), array("d", [1.0]))})` and `fake.index(None, [doc1], {"a": (array("q", [0]), array("d", [2.0]))})`, `fake.query(None, ["a"])` returns only the posting for `doc1` (ordinal 1), discarding the posting for `doc0`, even though `fake.docs` contains both docs. The earlier fix only made the docs list append and offset new ordinals; it does not merge postings for existing terms, so a test that indexes disjoint terms does not answer the original `index` contract.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/search.py:39

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_packed` validation raises on a foreign typecode, but `rebuild` performs its destructive deletes before calling `self.index`. On a connection where DML commits (for example `isolation_level=None`) or when the caller commits/uses the connection before rolling back, calling `rebuild(con, docs, {"t": (array("i", [0]), array("d", [1.0]))})` on an existing valid index executes `delete from similar_docs` and `delete from similar_terms`, then `_packed` raises `ValueError`. The previous index is therefore removed while the replacement postings are never written; a rebuild with invalid postings should be rejected before the destructive delete.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/search.py:SqliteSearchIndex.rebuild

chunk_findings.detail: `SqliteSearchIndex.index` inserts the new `similar_docs` rows before it validates or offsets the postings. The new `_packed(...)` call in the second `executemany` is now the place that rejects foreign array typecodes (the new test asserts it raises `ValueError`), but by the time `_packed` is evaluated the first `executemany` has already written every row in `docs`. For example, `idx.index(con, _DOCS, {"t": (array("i", [0]), array("d", [1.0]))})` inserts `len(_DOCS)` document rows, then raises `ValueError` without inserting any postings for `"t"` and without rolling back the adapter’s own work. If the caller catches that `ValueError` and retries with a valid `array("q")` posting, the next call sees `start == len(_DOCS)`, inserts duplicate docs, and offsets the new posting ordinals by the phantom first batch, so `query` can rank duplicate or unintended rows. The new foreign-typecode test hides this because it passes `docs=[]`; a non-empty `docs` call demonstrates that the changed `index` mutates the index before rejecting the input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/search.py:106

chunk_findings.detail: The new merge branch mutates the arrays already stored for a term in place. When a term is first added with `start == 0`, `off = ords`, so the fake stores the caller's own `ords` array; a later `index` call for the same term then executes `held[0].extend(off)`, appending to that caller array. For example, `postings = {"a": (array("q", [0]), array("d", [1.0]))}`; `idx.rebuild(None, [d0], postings)`; `idx.index(None, [d1], {"a": (array("q", [0]), array("d", [2.0]))})` leaves the caller's `postings["a"][0]` as `array("q", [0, 1])` and `postings["a"][1]` as `array("d", [1.0, 2.0])`, corrupting the input postings (and any earlier `query` result, because `query` returns these arrays by reference). The fake should copy or replace postings rather than extending held arrays in place.

chunk_findings.detail: `index` updates a term that is already indexed by mutating the arrays stored in `self.postings` in place (`held[0].extend(...)`, `held[1].extend(...)`), while `query` returns those same array objects. Thus a query result captured before an incremental index changes after the index. For example: `fake.index(None, [d1], {"a": (array("I", [0]), array("f", [1.0]))})`; `before = fake.query(None, ["a"])`; `fake.index(None, [d2], {"a": (array("I", [0]), array("f", [2.0]))})`; then `before["a"][0]` is now `array("I", [0, 1])` instead of the snapshot `array("I", [0])` that was returned. A query result should be stable with respect to later indexing (and the previous fake did not mutate earlier query results because `index` replaced postings), so this can make callers or tests see postings for documents that were not indexed when the query was made.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/search.py:FakeSearchIndex.index

chunk_findings.detail: The new incremental `index()` path offsets doc ordinals by `count(*)`, but it still writes every posting batch with a plain `insert into similar_terms`. It has no read/merge/update path for a term that already has postings. For example, after `idx.rebuild(con, [doc0], {"t": (array("q", [0]), array("d", [1.0]))})`, calling `idx.index(con, [doc1], {"t": (array("q", [0]), array("d", [0.5]))})}` inserts a second posting row for term `t` (or violates a term uniqueness constraint if `similar_terms.term` is unique). The unchanged `query()` API returns one `Postings` value per term, so the second batch is not merged into the first; ranking can silently miss `doc1`, or the call can fail with an `IntegrityError`. This contradicts the port behavior exercised by `test_the_fake_merges_a_term_already_indexed`, where indexing the same term again must produce merged ordinals `(0, 1)` and weights `(1.0, 2.0)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/search.py:SqliteSearchIndex.index
